opus-5.5.text:
I think the most honest way to assess it is to look at where we started and what we were trying to solve. When we first launched Cosmos, the core idea was that physical AI, robots, autonomous vehicles, any system that has to act in the real world, needs something like a world model. It needs to understand how the world evolves, how objects move, how actions lead to consequences. The first generation was really about proving that a video-based world foundation model could be useful to the physical AI community at all, and about releasing it openly so developers could build on it.

With Cosmos 3, I'd say the big step is that we're moving from "a model that can generate plausible videos of the world" toward "a model that actually understands and reasons about the physical world in a way that is useful for training and evaluating agents." That's a big shift. Generating pretty videos is one thing; generating videos that are physically consistent, controllable, and that you can trust enough to use as training data or as a simulator is a much harder bar.

So in terms of what I'm proud of: the integration of understanding and generation is much tighter, the controllability is better, so developers can condition on things like layouts, trajectories, or sensor inputs, and the physical plausibility has improved quite a lot. We also put a lot of effort into the data side, curating huge amounts of real-world video focused on physical interactions, because the model is only as good as what it learns from.

But I also want to be candid: we're still early. If you ask me whether world models today are as mature for physical AI as large language models are for language, the answer is no. There are still failure cases: long-horizon consistency, fine-grained contact physics, things like deformable objects and fluids. These are hard. I see Cosmos 3 as a meaningful milestone, not a finish line.

What makes me most excited is actually the adoption. Seeing robotics companies, AV teams, and researchers take the models, post-train them for their own domains, and come back with results we didn't anticipate — that's the real measure for me. Our goal was never just to build a model; it was to build a platform that accelerates the whole field. On that front, I think Cosmos 3 is doing what we hoped, and it gives us a much stronger foundation for what comes next.

r001.rationale: It describes tighter integration of understanding and generation, but does not say a unified Cosmos 3 model outperformed each previously separate model.

r002.rationale: It calls Cosmos 3 an early milestone and mentions remaining limitations, but does not attribute releasing it before full convergence to time constraints.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that I'm proud of it, but I also try to be careful about how I talk about it, because world models are still a young field and it's easy to overclaim.

If I step back, what we set out to do with Cosmos from the beginning was fairly simple to state and very hard to execute: build a foundation model that understands how the physical world evolves, so that robots and autonomous systems can learn from simulated experience instead of only from expensive, slow, sometimes dangerous real-world data. The first Cosmos was really about proving the recipe. We showed you could pretrain on an enormous amount of video, learn the physics implicitly, and then fine-tune for downstream tasks. The second generation was about making that useful, closing the gap between a pretty video and a video that is actually faithful enough to train a policy on.

With Cosmos 3, the thing I'm most happy about is that the model stopped being a demo and started being infrastructure. Two things changed. One is controllability. You can now condition on actions, on language, on camera trajectories, on structured inputs like depth or segmentation, and the model respects those constraints over long horizons much more reliably than before. For robotics that is the whole game. A world model that drifts after two seconds is a toy. A world model that stays physically consistent for the length of a manipulation task is a training environment. The second is that we invested very heavily in physical fidelity rather than just visual fidelity. Contact, occlusion, object permanence, things falling the way they should. These are unglamorous, but they are what practitioners actually complained about, and I think we moved the needle a lot.

Where I'm more measured is on what it means. People sometimes hear "world model" and imagine the model has a complete understanding of physics. It doesn't. It has a very strong statistical prior that is right most of the time and wrong in ways that are sometimes subtle. So I would say we achieved a big step toward making synthetic experience a first-class source of training data for physical AI. I would not say we've solved simulation. The gap between what the model produces and what a robot encounters in a real warehouse or a real kitchen is still real, and the next few years are about shrinking that gap and, just as importantly, measuring it rigorously.

The other achievement, which is maybe less visible from the outside, is the ecosystem. We open-sourced the models and the data pipelines, and the number of groups, academic and industrial, that are now building on top of Cosmos rather than starting from scratch is something I find genuinely meaningful. I spent a long time in research watching good ideas die because the compute wasn't there. If Cosmos 3 lets a small robotics lab do work that used to require a large company's resources, that is the part I would be most proud of, more than any benchmark number.

r001.rationale: The response describes improved controllability and physical fidelity, but does not say a unified Cosmos 3 model outperformed each previously separate model.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute releasing Cosmos 3 before full convergence to time constraints.

astra-6.text: I would assess it by asking how much closer we’ve brought the technology to being useful. It’s one thing to produce an impressive demo; it’s another to deliver something people can reliably build on. For Cosmos 3, I’d look at the quality of the results, how consistently it handles difficult cases, and whether it helps users accomplish something they couldn’t do before. I’d also be careful to distinguish progress from problems we’ve fully solved. The limitations matter just as much as the successes when we decide what to work on next.

sol-6.1.text: I think the way to assess Cosmos 3 is to ask whether it moves us closer to useful world models. Can the model capture how the physical world behaves, generalize to situations it hasn’t seen, and help us build better embodied AI systems? Visual quality matters, but it’s only part of the picture. Ultimately, the test is whether these models help robots and other physical AI systems perform better in the real world. That’s the standard I would use to judge our progress.
